cards.front: Peyton Rous passed ground chicken sarcoma tissue through a filter proven to stop bacteria, injected the clear filtrate into healthy hens, and observed new sarcomas. What did this show?
cards.back: An agent smaller than a bacterium—the size of a virus—carried the cancer from bird to bird.
cards.why: Because the filter held back bacteria, only a sub-bacterial agent passing into the filtrate could trigger tumours at the needle site.
cards.quote: Something smaller than a bacterium, the size of a virus, had carried the cancer from bird to bird—all the filter could say
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: A gene that can turn a cell cancerous is an {{c1::oncogene}}.
cards.quote: A gene that can turn a cell cancerous is an oncogene.
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: A normal gene that can become an oncogene when altered is a {{c1::proto-oncogene}}.
cards.quote: A normal gene that can become an oncogene when altered is a proto-oncogene.
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: Dominique Stehelin's radioactive single-stranded DNA probe for viral src stuck to DNA from uninfected chickens. Why could that result alone not prove src was a normal bird gene?
cards.back: It fit two competing hypotheses: an ancient viral infection left behind in chicken chromosomes, or a normal bird gene the virus had picked up.
cards.quote: It stuck to DNA from uninfected chickens—yet that alone fit two competing hypotheses: an ancient viral infection left behind in chicken chromosomes
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: Stehelin tested a src probe and a probe for Rous sarcoma virus's other genes on DNA from an evolutionarily distant bird (an emu). What pattern does the cellular-gene hypothesis predict, and why?
cards.back: The src probe should still match emu DNA closely while the probe for the rest of the virus matches poorly, because a normal bird gene is conserved across distant bird lineages whereas a chicken-specific viral infection is not.
cards.quote: A cellular gene predicts that the src probe should still match emu DNA closely while the rest of the virus matches poorly outside chickens.
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: Why is viral v-Src stuck active compared with the normal cellular tyrosine kinase c-Src?
cards.back: Normal c-Src clamps itself shut when its SH2 domain grips a phosphorylated tail tyrosine (tyrosine 527 in chicken); v-Src lacks that tail tyrosine, so nothing closes the clamp.
cards.why: A few changes elsewhere in v-Src raise its kinase activity further.
cards.quote: In v-Src the tail is replaced and that tyrosine is gone, so nothing closes the clamp, and a few changes elsewhere raise its activity further.
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: A tyrosine kinase is normally held shut because its own binding domain grips a phosphorylated tyrosine near its tail. A mutation replaces the tail so that tyrosine is lost, leaving the catalytic site intact. What happens to kinase activity, and why?
cards.back: The kinase sticks on. Without the phosphorylated tail tyrosine for the binding domain to grip, the autoinhibitory clamp cannot close.
cards.quote: c-Src clamps itself shut when its SH2 domain grips a phosphorylated tail tyrosine (tyrosine 527 in chicken).
cards.section: The story: the cancer gene was the chicken's own

cards.front: What are the five molecular routes by which a signalling switch can stick on in cancer?
cards.back: Breaking a protein's off-step by one amino acid change; losing an inhibitory clamp; copying a normal gene too many times; joining two genes; and losing an off-protein.
cards.quote: Jamming an on-step or removing an off-step—pushing a cell to divide unless its checkpoints stop it—falls into five molecular routes across this course:
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: In some breast cancers, the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase gene is copied many times over with its normal sequence. How do these unmutated receptors signal strongly without growth factor?
cards.back: Receptor tyrosine kinases activate when two receptors pair and phosphorylate each other; crowding too many normal HER2 receptors into the membrane lets them pair unaided.
cards.quote: Receptor tyrosine kinases switch on when two receptors pair and phosphorylate each other.
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: Normal cells with ordinary, unamplified levels of HER2 are deprived of all growth factors, including ligands for EGFR. What happens to HER2 signalling, and why?
cards.back: HER2 signalling should stay off. HER2 has no growth factor of its own and normally pairs with a relative such as EGFR after that partner binds ligand.
cards.quote: HER2 has no growth factor of its own—normally it pairs with a relative such as EGFR after that partner binds ligand
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: In the BCR-ABL fusion protein of chronic myeloid leukaemia, what receptor tyrosine kinase step does the BCR segment imitate?
cards.back: Ligand-driven pairing: BCR makes the fusion proteins stick together so the ABL kinase domains sit side by side and switch each other on.
cards.quote: In BCR-ABL, the BCR segment makes the fusion proteins stick together, imitating ligand-driven pairing.
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: A chromosomal rearrangement fuses an unrelated self-binding protein segment to a tyrosine kinase whose catalytic site is completely unmutated. What happens to the kinase's activity, and why?
cards.back: The kinase switches on without upstream input. The fused partner holds two kinase domains side by side so they switch each other on, imitating ligand-driven pairing without mutating the catalytic site.
cards.quote: Rows three and four activate a tyrosine kinase without mutating its catalytic site.
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: A gene whose loss lets cells grow when they should not is a {{c1::tumour suppressor}}.
cards.quote: A gene whose loss lets cells grow when they should not is a tumour suppressor.
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: For the tumour suppressors PTEN, neurofibromin, and APC, what signalling molecule does each normally clear or turn off?
cards.back: PTEN removes the phosphate that makes PIP3; neurofibromin is a GAP for Ras; APC helps mark β-catenin for destruction.
cards.quote: PTEN removes the phosphate PI 3-kinase adds to make PIP3, neurofibromin is a GAP for Ras, and APC helps mark β-catenin for destruction.
cards.section: The idea: five ways to stick a switch

cards.front: In a diploid cell, why does a gain-of-function oncogene mutation act when only one gene copy is altered?
cards.back: One altered or amplified copy signals without input and the normal copy cannot shut it off, making it a dominant gain of function.
cards.quote: one altered or amplified copy signals without input and the normal copy cannot shut it off—a dominant gain of function.
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: In a diploid cell, why is loss of a tumour suppressor off-switch usually recessive at the cellular level?
cards.back: One working copy usually supplies enough off-protein to restrain the pathway, so both copies usually must be lost for the switch to stick on.
cards.quote: one working copy usually supplies enough off-protein, so loss is usually recessive inside the cell:
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: With no growth factor present, diploid Cell A has one always-on Ras copy and one normal copy, while Cell B has one lost Ras-GAP copy and one normal copy. What is the pathway state in each cell, and why?
cards.back: Stuck on in Cell A; usually off in Cell B. One always-on Ras acts dominantly because normal Ras cannot turn it off, whereas one working Ras-GAP copy usually supplies enough off-protein.
cards.quote: For rows one to four, one altered or amplified copy signals without input and the normal copy cannot shut it off—a dominant gain of function.
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: Retinoblastoma occurs in an inherited form (born with one broken tumour suppressor copy) and a non-inherited form (born with two working copies). Which form appears earlier and follows single-chance-event timing, and why?
cards.back: The inherited form. Every retinal cell already carries the first hit and needs only one later chance event to lose the second copy, whereas two working copies require two independent hits in the same cell.
cards.quote: A child born with one broken copy already has the first hit in every retinal cell, so only one later chance event is needed
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: Why do tumour mutations cluster at a few specific positions in an oncogene like Ras, whereas tumour suppressor mutations scatter along the gene?
cards.back: Few specific changes can jam a protein into an active state, whereas many different changes along the gene can break an off-protein.
cards.quote: The same asymmetry shapes where mutations fall: because few changes jam a protein on while many break it
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: Activating tumour mutations in Ras cluster at positions 12, 13, and {{c1::61}}.
cards.quote: tumour mutations in Ras cluster at positions 12, 13 and 61, whereas tumour suppressor mutations scatter along the gene
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: Sequencing hundreds of tumours shows that Gene A is mutated almost exclusively at two codons on one allele, while Gene B has inactivating mutations scattered across its length affecting both alleles. How should Genes A and B be classified, and why?
cards.back: Gene A is most likely a proto-oncogene (dominant gain of function) and Gene B a tumour suppressor (recessive loss of function). Few changes jam a switch on, so one altered copy clusters at hotspots, whereas many scattered changes break an off-protein, which usually needs both copies lost.
cards.quote: tumour mutations in Ras cluster at positions 12, 13 and 61, whereas tumour suppressor mutations scatter along the gene
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: A translocation on one chromosome fuses a self-binding partner to the kinase domain of a receptor tyrosine kinase while the second allele stays normal. Predict whether (1) the kinase catalytic site must also be mutated and (2) the second allele must be lost for the switch to stick on.
cards.back: (1) No catalytic-site mutation is needed: by the gene-fusion route rule, the self-binding partner holds kinase domains side by side to switch each other on. (2) The second allele need not be lost: by the diploid copy-number rule, one altered copy acts as a dominant gain of function because the normal copy cannot shut it off.
cards.quote: For rows one to four, one altered or amplified copy signals without input and the normal copy cannot shut it off—a dominant gain of function.
cards.section: One copy or two: gain acts alone, loss needs both

cards.front: In fresh primary rat embryo cells, introducing always-on ras alone or myc alone fails to transform the cells, whereas introducing both together transforms them. What does this experiment show?
cards.back: Transforming normal primary cells requires cooperating changes rather than a single stuck growth switch.
cards.quote: Neither ras alone nor myc alone transformed the fresh embryo cells; only both together did, because transformation here needs two cooperating changes.
cards.section: Why one stuck switch is not enough

cards.front: Why is a single nonstop growth signal seldom enough to turn a normal cell into a tumour?
cards.back: In normal cells, p53 treats excess growth signalling like damaged DNA to halt or kill the cell, and cells escaping p53 still need survival signals or die by apoptosis.
cards.quote: halting or killing the cell, and cells escaping p53 still need survival signals (the cell death lesson) or die by apoptosis.
cards.section: Why one stuck switch is not enough

cards.front: In colon tumours, a common order of cooperating changes is loss of {{c1::APC}} early, always-on Ras later, and loss of p53 later still.
cards.quote: in the colon a common order is loss of APC early, always-on Ras later and loss of p53 later still.
cards.section: Why one stuck switch is not enough

cards.front: A person inherits one broken copy of APC, and a single colon cell later loses its second APC copy. Using the lesson's rules on off-switch loss and tumour progression, predict whether that cell immediately forms a full tumour, and explain why.
cards.back: Usually no. By the two-hit off-switch rule, losing both APC copies stops β-catenin clearance and jams one growth switch; however, by the cooperating-changes rule, checkpoints such as p53 and apoptosis still restrain normal cells until later cooperating changes (commonly always-on Ras and then p53 loss) accumulate.
cards.quote: Tumours therefore accumulate cooperating changes; in the colon a common order is loss of APC early, always-on Ras later and loss of p53 later still.
cards.section: Why one stuck switch is not enough

cards.front: A multi-mutation tumour's reliance on a single stuck signalling switch is called {{c1::oncogene addiction}}.
cards.quote: This dependence, oncogene addiction, explains why a drug targeting one protein—above all imatinib against BCR-ABL
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: In mice with a tumour driven by an engineered switchable oncogene, switching off that single oncogene shrinks the tumour even though its other mutations stay unchanged. What does this show?
cards.back: The tumour cells depend on that one signal (oncogene addiction) to keep dividing or survive, despite carrying multiple other mutations.
cards.quote: tumours that grew with it on have shrunk when it was turned off, although their other mutations were unchanged—the cells stopped dividing or died.
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: What two non-exclusive ideas are proposed to explain oncogene addiction?
cards.back: Chronic negative feedback from the stuck pathway keeps feedback inhibitors high and may quiet parallel routes, or survival signals fade faster than death signals once the oncogene shuts off.
cards.quote: a stuck pathway keeps feedback inhibitors high and may quiet parallel routes, or survival signals fading faster than death signals once the oncogene shuts off.
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: If chronic negative feedback keeps a tumour addicted to one oncogene, what happens to feedback inhibitors and parallel growth pathways after a drug shuts that oncogene off, and what does this imply for resistance?
cards.back: Feedback inhibitors can fall, waking previously quieted parallel growth pathways. Surviving cells—or cells gaining a parallel mutation—may then use another pathway to resume growth.
cards.quote: After the drug shuts the oncogene off, those inhibitors can fall, so surviving cells—or cells gaining a parallel mutation—may wake another pathway and resume growth.
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: In a tumour model, parallel growth pathways are unusually quiet before drug treatment; after a drug shuts off the driver oncogene, feedback inhibitors drop, parallel pathways switch on, and surviving clones later regrow. Which addiction model fits these data, and which rule explains the regrowth?
cards.back: The chronic negative feedback model fits these data. By the feedback-addiction rule, a stuck oncogene keeps feedback inhibitors high and quiets parallel routes before treatment; once the drug turns the oncogene off, falling inhibitors allow surviving or newly mutated cells to wake a parallel pathway and resume growth.
cards.quote: Before the drug arrives, high feedback inhibitors should quiet parallel growth pathways. After the drug shuts the oncogene off, those inhibitors can fall
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: A tumour carries both a stuck oncogenic kinase and loss of both p53 copies. A student argues that a drug blocking only that kinase cannot shrink the tumour because p53 is still absent. Evaluate this argument.
cards.back: The argument is not sound. Tumours usually need several changes (including p53 loss), yet a multi-mutation tumour can still depend on one stuck switch (oncogene addiction), so a drug blocking that kinase can sometimes shrink it even with p53 still absent.
cards.quote: though tumours usually need several changes, they often depend on one stuck switch.
cards.section: A tumour that needs its oncogene

cards.front: In the receptor → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK chain, one copy of the gene for a phosphatase that strips phosphate from ERK is deleted while the second copy stays normal. With no growth factor present, what happens to ERK activity, and why?
cards.back: ERK usually stays off. The phosphatase is an off-switch, so one working copy usually supplies enough enzyme and both copies usually must be lost for ERK to stick on.
cards.quote: Both copies usually must be lost (loss). The GAP for Ras, neurofibromin. The phosphatases that strip phosphate from the receptor, MEK or ERK.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the receptor → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK chain, a single copy of Raf carries a mutation (such as BRAF V600E) fixing it in its active shape. With no growth factor present, what happens to ERK, and why?
cards.back: ERK sticks on. A Raf fixed in its active shape is a dominant gain of function, so one altered copy signals through MEK to ERK without growth factor.
cards.quote: A Raf or a MEK fixed in its active shape (BRAF V600E, common in melanoma, is one).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why are inherited cancer risks more often caused by a lost off-switch than by a strongly stuck on-switch?
cards.back: Because an inherited change affects every cell, a strongly stuck on-switch disturbs the embryo, whereas one lost off-switch copy is mostly silent until a second hit.
cards.quote: A strongly stuck on-switch in every cell disturbs the embryo, and the milder inherited activating changes in this pathway cause developmental syndromes called RASopathies.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Milder inherited activating changes in the receptor–Ras–ERK pathway cause developmental syndromes called {{c1::RASopathies}}.
cards.quote: the milder inherited activating changes in this pathway cause developmental syndromes called RASopathies.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: As an exception to the usual off-switch pattern of inherited cancer risk, inherited activating changes in the receptor {{c1::RET}} cause a cancer syndrome.
cards.quote: There are exceptions: inherited activating changes in the receptor RET cause a cancer syndrome.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a growth-factor pathway, compare (1) one copy of a receptor missing its outer part so it pairs without ligand against (2) one inherited dead copy of the ligase that tags active receptors for removal, both inside a single cell and as an inherited cancer risk.
cards.back: By the diploid copy-number rule, the truncated receptor is a dominant gain of function (one copy leaves the pathway stuck on), whereas one dead ligase copy is recessive inside a cell (the second copy still tags active receptors). By the inherited-risk rule, a strongly stuck receptor in every cell disturbs the embryo, while one dead ligase copy is mostly silent until a second hit occurs in one of billions of cells.
cards.quote: The ligase that tags an active receptor for removal. Inherited risk. Expect the loss kind more often.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In chronic myeloid leukaemia, a reciprocal chromosomal swap moves ABL from chromosome 9 beside BCR on chromosome {{c1::22}}.
cards.quote: later work showed the reciprocal swap places ABL from chromosome 9 beside BCR on chromosome 22.
cards.section: How the BCR-ABL join was found

cards.front: Ras S17N stays locked in its GDP-bound form. If one copy of Ras S17N is expressed alongside normal Ras, what happens to normal Ras activation by one model, and why?
cards.back: Normal Ras activation is impaired despite one normal copy remaining. By one model, GDP-locked Ras S17N interferes with normal Ras by tying up the exchange factor normal Ras needs.
cards.quote: Ras S17N stays in its GDP form and, by one model, ties up the exchange factor normal Ras needs
cards.section: Exceptions to the one-copy rules

cards.front: A tumour suppressor such as p53 functions as a tetramer. Compare a cell with one normal copy and one missense mutant copy that still joins the complex against a cell with one normal copy and one deleted copy. Which impairs function more, and why?
cards.back: The missense mutant impairs function more. Many p53 missense mutants act as dominant negatives by poisoning the tetramer they form with wild-type subunits, whereas a single deleted copy leaves wild-type subunits unpoisoned.
cards.quote: many p53 missense mutants poison the tetramer they form with wild-type subunits as dominant negatives.
cards.section: Exceptions to the one-copy rules

cards.front: In mice, mutant Kras tumours often later lose their remaining normal Kras copy; meanwhile, a single p53 missense mutant copy can disable p53 function while the normal copy remains. Explain how each case departs from the simple copy-number rule.
cards.back: The simple rule treats a gain-of-function oncogene as unaffected by the normal copy and an off-switch loss as requiring both copies gone. Mutant Kras departs via normal-copy restraint (normal Kras restrains mutant-Kras tumours in mice until lost), while p53 missense departs via dominant-negative interference (mutant subunits poison the wild-type tetramer through one copy).
cards.quote: The normal copy is not always irrelevant: in mice, normal Kras restrains tumours driven by mutant Kras, and such tumours often lose the normal copy later.
cards.section: Exceptions to the one-copy rules

cards.front: Mice that have lost only one copy of the tumour suppressor PTEN show measurable pathway effects even while their second copy remains intact. Which assumption of two-hit kinetics does this finding break, and how does it relate to the copy-number rule?
cards.back: It breaks the assumption that one working copy of an off-switch always supplies enough protein to restrain the pathway. Under the lesson's copy-number rule, off-switch loss is usually recessive in diploid cells, so PTEN dosage effects in mice represent an exception where halving gene dose already alters signalling.
cards.quote: two-hit kinetics assume one copy supplies enough protein: PTEN shows dosage effects in mice
cards.section: Exceptions to the one-copy rules
